name: Cowley et al. 2024 Nature knockout training of LC neurons and Drosophila visual pursuit (LC10, courtship)
bibliography: [1] Cowley B.R., Calhoun A.J., Rangarajan N., Ireland E., Turner M.H., Pillow J.W., Murthy M. (2024). Mapping model units to visual neurons reveals population code for social behaviour. Nature 629(8014):1100-1108. DOI 10.1038/s41586-024-07451-8; open access PMC11136655 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11136655/), PMID 38778103. Code, saved model weights, fictive-female stimulus generator: https://github.com/murthylab/one2one-mapping (public, GPL-3.0, TensorFlow notebooks). Data: DANDI dandiset 000951 (dandiarchive.org/dandiset/000951). Preprint (same study, earlier version): Cowley et al. 2023 bioRxiv, 'One-to-one mapping between deep network units and real neurons uncovers a visual population code for social behavior' (CSHL repository eprint 41557) - duplicate of [1]. [2] Ribeiro I.M.A., Drews M., Bahl A., Machacek C., Borst A., Dickson B.J. (2018). Visual projection neurons mediating directed courtship in Drosophila. Cell 174(3):607-621. DOI 10.1016/j.cell.2018.06.020 (Dickson/Borst labs, not Murthy lab as the task title implies). No model code. [3] Hindmarsh Sten T., Li R., Otopalik A., Ruta V. (2021). Sexual arousal gates visual processing during Drosophila courtship. Nature 595:549-553. DOI 10.1038/s41586-021-03714-w; PMC8973426. Preprint duplicate: bioRxiv 10.1101/2020.08.31.275883 ('An arousal-gated visual circuit controls pursuit during Drosophila courtship'). Model code 'available on request' (no public repository found).
full_text_checked: [1] Full text of PMC version read (main text, Methods incl. architecture, rendering, training, limitations; figure legends via text); Extended Data figures and supplementary only via text references; GitHub repository landing page checked (folders saved_models, stimuli, code, data), code files themselves not read. [2] Only abstract-level summary and secondary pages (MPG press, LMU project pages); full text not accessed. [3] bioRxiv full-text HTML first half read (results, model description); Methods partly truncated, Supplementary Table 1 (sample sizes) and journal version not accessed (PMC blocked by browser check).
task_and_output: [1] Predict moment-to-moment behaviour of a courting male Drosophila from its reconstructed visual input: outputs are forward, lateral and angular velocity (regression) and probabilities of sine song, Pfast and Pslow pulse song (classification) for the next frame. Internally, a 23-unit bottleneck whose units are assigned one-to-one to 23 lobula columnar (LC/LPLC) types; after training, model LC unit responses to fictive female stimuli (varying position, size, rotation) are compared to calcium responses of real LC types. No object localisation output (no centroid/box); female identity is never encoded as a choice - only one female exists. [2] Behavioural/physiological: LC10 silencing/activation effects on orienting, following, ipsilateral wing extension; LC10 tuning to small moving objects. [3] Tethered male pursuit (turning) of a virtual target; LC10a calcium gain; integrate-and-fire network model output = turn direction/strength from hemispheric LC10a spike count comparison.
data_and_independent_videos: [1] 459 courtship sessions of freely walking male-female pairs in a circular chamber with 16 microphones; 23 LC-silenced genotypes plus control, each with >12 sessions; females blind and pheromone-insensitive (PIBL). About 11.6 million training samples; each LC type and control capped at 600,000 frames; validation and test sets 27,000 frames (15 min) per LC type and control, sampled as 3 s windows held out from training. Split is by time windows within the same pool of sessions, not by unseen flies or sessions [uncertain: exact session-level separation not stated in the parts read]. Neural validation: two-photon imaging of 5 LC types (LC6, LC11, LC12, LC15, LC17) in head-fixed walking males, plus about 20 LC types from a prior female dataset (Extended Data Fig. 7a). [3] Tethered males on ball with projected virtual target; free-courtship validation of the model on 6 pairs; other n in Supplementary Table 1 (not accessed).
target_size_and_input_resolution: [1] Input frames rendered at 64 x 256 pixels, trimmed to 64 x 228 after removing the 40 deg behind the male; field of view about 160 deg each side, i.e. roughly 1.4 deg per pixel horizontally [uncertain: derived, not stated]. Female rendered as grey ellipses (head, eyes, thorax, tail, no wings) on uniform white background; female 'size 1.0' corresponds to about 65 deg visual angle when she faces away at the centre, so the target is typically large (tens of pixels wide), not a few-pixel object. Grey 1-channel image. [3] Target is a high-contrast dot approximating a female's angular size [uncertain: exact degrees not read]; LC10a tuned to small moving targets over a range of sizes; model LC10a array covers about 270 deg with about 15 deg binocular overlap. [2] LC10 prefers small moving objects via antagonistic motion-based centre-surround.
frame_rate_and_camera_motion: [1] 30 Hz; model input = 10 most recent frames (about 300 ms), same convolution weights per frame (temporal 3D convolution variant did not improve prediction). Egocentric frames reconstructed from SLEAP-tracked joints of both flies, so male self-motion only changes where the female appears; there is no background texture, hence no background optic flow; male head/body motion not an input. [3] Tethered male, closed/open-loop virtual target on conical screen; widefield optomotor motion used only as control showing LC10a gain change is specific to target tracking.
detector_and_exemplar: [1] No detector and no exemplar: the female's pose is given by SLEAP tracking and re-rendered, so the network sees a clean single target by construction; target identity is implicit (only object in scene). [3] No detector; single synthetic dot (or two dots in distractor tests).
trainable_nodes_and_loss: [1] Everything trained end to end, none biologically constrained: vision network (3x3 conv 32 filters stride 2, then two separable 2D convs, batchnorm+ReLU, linear mapping to 16 embedding variables per frame, shared over 10 frames) -> dense 64 -> 23-unit ReLU LC bottleneck -> decision network of 3 dense layers x 128 -> linear velocity outputs and sigmoid song outputs. Loss: MSE (velocities) + binary cross-entropy (song). SGD lr 1e-3, momentum 0.7, batch 288, early stopping on validation forward velocity; left-right flip augmentation with sign flip of lateral/angular velocity. Knockout training: for frames from a male of silenced LC type k, model unit k is clamped to 0; for control frames nothing is clamped; unit-to-type assignment arbitrary at initialisation. Parameter count not given [uncertain: total parameters]. [3] Network model hand-designed (integrate-and-fire LC10a with receptive fields from Ribeiro 2018 plus downstream hemispheric comparison), P1-dependent gain parameter; no deep training.
controls_seeds_splits: [1] Controls: dropout-trained network (random unit dropout instead of type-specific knockout), network trained without knockout (noKO), untrained network, GLM baselines on movement history, song history and visual history. 10 random initialisations: knockout beat dropout in 8/10 runs and noKO in 5/10 runs for forward velocity (i.e. prediction gain from knockout is not robust against noKO); ensemble of 10 KO networks used to estimate uncertainty of predicted responses. Held-out 3 s windows for test. Authors note results vary across training runs. [3] Two-target and pause stimuli, widefield motion control, unilateral silencing/activation, P1 activation by CsChrimson; tethered-female control (9 females).
metrics_and_numbers: [1] Held-out frame-wise prediction: forward velocity R2 about 0.5; lateral and angular velocity R2 about 0.15 (Fig. 1, main text); song scored as 1 - BCE (values not extracted). Predicted vs real mean behavioural changes across 23 silenced types correlate (Fig. 1g-h, n = 23). Neural prediction of calcium responses (noise-corrected R2): about 0.35 with fixed one-to-one unit mapping vs about 0.65 with fitted linear mapping (Fig. 2). Encoding (Fig. 3e): most LC units encode female position, about half encode size, rotation weakly; about 25% of response variance on average from nonlinear interactions among position, size, rotation. Examples (Fig. 3d,f,g): LC31 position; LPLC2 looming size and speed; LC10a position only when male close and behind female, plus size; LC17 delayed size; LC13 speed of size change. Fig. 4: single-unit inactivation has little effect; behaviour depends on combinations (population code). Seeds: KO > dropout 8/10, KO > noKO 5/10 (forward velocity). [3] P1 activity correlates with tracking index r = 0.562 +/- 0.092 but not with stimulus r = 0.004 +/- 0.006; network model predicts tethered turning to pause stimulus r = 0.86 and to two drifting targets r = 0.83; free courtship steering over minutes mean r = 0.52 +/- 0.06 (6 pairs); model insensitive to angular size; removing binocular overlap or direction selectivity degrades it (bioRxiv figures 4-5 [uncertain: exact figure numbers]).
tested_conditions: [1] Unseen videos: partially - test frames are held-out 3 s windows, unseen flies/sessions not reported [uncertain]. Target absence: not reported (female always present; frames without female not analysed as a refusal task). Similar distractors: no (single female, no second fly). Occlusion: not reported (rendering of a single female; self-occlusion only). Night or low light: no (uniform white background, clean rendering). Sequential operation on own predictions: no (one-step prediction from true visual history, no closed loop). [3] Unseen videos: model validated on free courtship (6 pairs) - yes in a limited sense. Target absence: pause stimulus only (target stops, not disappears) - not tested as absence. Similar distractors: yes - two targets (second at 98% velocity or opposite position); LC10a responses persist and model predicts turning r = 0.83, but no identity selection mechanism beyond hemispheric competition. Occlusion: not reported. Low light: no. Sequential/closed-loop: tethered pursuit is closed loop in behaviour, model not run on its own predictions [uncertain]. [2] Only behavioural and physiological tests; no distractor or low-light tests reported in parts read.
mechanism_summary: Published: (a) Cowley 2024 - a learned narrow bottleneck of 23 non-negative units between a generic CNN front end and a behaviour decoder; knockout training (clamping unit k to zero exactly on data from flies with LC type k silenced) uses perturbation data to pin each unit's role, and after training each unit's tuning to female position/size/rotation can be read out. The finding is that the single social target is represented by a distributed population code: position in most units, size in about half, rotation weakly, with nonlinear mixing; no single LC type carries the target. (b) Ribeiro 2018 - LC10 neurons are tuned to small moving objects by an antagonistic motion centre-surround, and are necessary and (unilaterally) sufficient for orienting to the female. (c) Hindmarsh Sten 2021 - an internal state signal (P1 arousal) multiplicatively raises LC10a gain to moving fly-sized targets without changing tuning shape; a simple hemispheric comparison of LC10a activity predicts steering. Proposed modification (ours, not published): add an LC-like small-object bottleneck readout on top of FlyVis T4/T5/Tm/LC-input cell activity and a state-dependent gain (P1-like) driven by tracker confidence in the previous target.
transfer_limits: (1) Single clean target by construction: input is a re-rendered ellipse female on white background from tracked keypoints; no clutter, no similar neighbours, no low light, no camera noise - our core failure (choosing the previous target among similar neighbours, refusing when absent) is untested here. (2) Target scale: female up to about 65 deg in a 64 x 228 image covering 320 deg, i.e. large relative to the field, versus our targets about 9 x 12 lattice steps inside 721 grey hexals of a moving, rescaling crop. (3) Self-motion: egocentric re-rendering with no background means no ego-motion flow; our 30 Hz crops from a moving camera have strong background motion, which LC10-type centre-surround is meant to suppress but which Cowley's model never faced. (4) 30 Hz and 10-frame history do match our rate, but frames are clean and the model predicts behaviour, not position; no localisation or confidence output. (5) The front end is a generic CNN, not FlyVis: model 'LC units' are only weakly mapped to real LC responses (noise-corrected R2 about 0.35 one-to-one), so it is not a validated FlyVis-downstream circuit. (6) Knockout training needs perturbation data (silenced flies); we have no analogue for BDD100K except artificial ablation of FlyVis cell types, which would be an analysis method, not supervision. (7) Identity: the population code encodes where/how big the one target is, not which of several look-alike objects it is; for our YOLO/ByteTrack/MASA environment the needed function is association/re-identification, which these sources do not address except the two-dot hemispheric competition in [3]. (8) Gain gating (P1) in [3] gives a principled 'attention to the current target' signal but is shown only for synthetic dots on a projector.
research_questions_addressed: Q1: caution/design analogy - shows how one target's position and size are carried in a population of LC-like units and that internal-state gain can select pursuit, but provides no exemplar-based identification among similar objects and no refusal; the two-target test in Hindmarsh Sten is the only distractor evidence and resolves by hemispheric competition, not identity. Q2: design analogy for diagnostics - knockout/ablation of named units and per-unit tuning probes (position/size/rotation) are a clean way to ask whether information is present in an intermediate representation versus lost in readout; Cowley's controls (noKO, dropout, untrained network, GLM baselines, 10 seeds) are a template for separating representation from readout and training. Q3: direct but limited - 30 Hz, 10 frames history, large clean targets, no background motion; does not cover small targets on moving cluttered backgrounds. Q4: not addressed (no confidence or localisation-quality output). Q5: design analogy - a 23-unit non-negative bottleneck plus small decoder is cheap (fits easily in 12 GB) and the noKO / dropout / untrained-network contrasts map to our B (no FlyVis) / C (frozen FlyVis) comparisons.
candidate_node_change: Node: readout of FlyVis (an LC-like bottleneck as part of our FlyVis version, connecting FlyVis output cell types to a small number of non-negative 'LC' units with retinotopic pooling constrained by FlyWire LC input wiring, e.g. LC10a/LC11/LC12/LC15-like pools from Lo/Li and T2/T3/Tm inputs, plus a multiplicative gain from the tracker's previous-target state, P1-like). Training: units trained to predict the offset and size of the previous target in the crop and a presence score; 'knockout training' analogue = during training clamp FlyVis cell-type groups to zero on random batches and record which LC unit loses information, used as a diagnostic not as supervision. Control without FlyVis: same bottleneck and decoder on raw 721-hexal grey input or a matched-parameter CNN (variant B). Control with stock FlyVis: same bottleneck on frozen stock FlyVis outputs (C) vs our modified FlyVis (D); add untrained/shuffled-weight FlyVis as null. Minimal check: on cached crops, linear/bottleneck probe of target offset and size from stock FlyVis vs raw input on held-out val videos; then one HOTA run with the 3-variant protocol (stand / readout without fly / readout with fly). Stop condition: if the bottleneck on FlyVis does not beat the same bottleneck on raw input by more than bootstrap CI for offset error on unseen videos, or HOTA (3) is not above (2), stop this readout and record; do not add more diagnostics (rule 6.16). Caution: by AGENTS.md boundary a head over FlyVis signal is 'application', not modernisation, unless the bottleneck is built from FlyVis/connectome LC wiring and becomes part of the fly model; the source supports only the wiring-agnostic version.
strongest_objection: The Cowley model is a generic CNN plus learned bottleneck trained on clean, single-target renderings to predict behaviour; its LC units are only loosely matched to real LC neurons and its 'population code' is a property of a flexible DNN under knockout constraints (knockout beat noKO in only 5 of 10 seeds for forward velocity). It gives no evidence that an LC-like bottleneck helps localise or re-identify one target among similar ones in cluttered, moving, low-light video, which is exactly our failure mode; adopting it risks building another readout head that a matched non-FlyVis head equals.
evidence_strength: [1] Peer-reviewed (Nature 2024), open access, public code and weights (GitHub murthylab/one2one-mapping verified public; files not run), data on DANDI; no independent replication known. Moderate for the population-code claim within its setting; weak for transfer to our task. [2] Peer-reviewed Cell 2018, physiological and genetic evidence, strong for LC10 small-object role; no code. [3] Peer-reviewed Nature 2021, strong physiology for arousal gain on LC10a; model code only on request; moderate. Overall for our decision: weak-to-moderate (design analogy and caution, not direct evidence).
